name: Matter of A-B-
holding: (1) Matter of A-R-C-G-, 26 I&N Dec. 338 (BIA 2014) is overruled. That decision was wrongly decided and should not have been issued as a precedential decision.

(2) An applicant seeking to establish persecution on account of membership in a 'particular social group' must demonstrate: (1) membership in a group, which is composed of members who share a common immutable characteristic, is defined with particularity, and is socially distinct within the society in question; and (2) that membership in the group is a central reason for her persecution. When the alleged persecutor is someone unaffiliated with the government, the applicant must also show that her home government is unwilling or unable to protect her.

(3) An asylum applicant has the burden of showing her eligibility for asylum. The applicant must present facts that establish each element of the standard, and the asylum officer, immigration judge, or the Board has the duty to determine whether those facts satisfy all of those elements.
(4) If an asylum application is fatally flawed in one respect, an immigration judge or the Board need not examine the remaining elements of the asylum claim.
(5) The mere fact that a country may have problems effectively policing certain crimes or that certain populations are more likely to be victims of crime, cannot itself establish an asylum claim.
(6) To be cognizable, a particular social group must exist independently of the harm asserted in an application for asylum.

(7) An applicant seeking to establish persecution based on violent conduct of a private actor must show more than the government's difficulty controlling private behavior. The applicant must show that the government condoned the private actions or demonstrated an inability to protect the victims.
(8) An applicant seeking asylum based on membership in a particular social group must clearly indicate on the record the exact delineation of any proposed particular social group.

(9) The Board, immigration judges, and all asylum officers must consider, consistent with the regulations, whether internal relocation in the alien's home country presents a reasonable alternative before granting asylum.
summary: Matter of A-B- was issued by Attorney General Sessions, during the first Trump administration. This is an example of the lesser common types of immigration case law: decisions plucked from the standard appeals process, BIA > District Court > Supreme Court, and is decided by the Attorney General.
notes: The procedural history of this case is 'a lotta ins, a lotta outs'. It's an incredibly powerful, sweeping set of decisions. For a cryptic overview of its history and eventual replacement by, well, the case law that preceded it (Matter of A-R-C-G-), see here: https://www.justice.gov/eoir/page/file/1404796/dl

name: Matter of H-A-A-V
holding: If the factual allegations underlying a claim for asylum, withholding of removal, or protection under the Convention Against Torture, viewed in the light most favorable to the respondent, do not establish prima facie eligibility for relief or protection, an Immigration Judge may pretermit the applications without a full evidentiary hearing on the merits of the claim.

name: Matter of K-E-S-G
holding: A particular social group defined by the alien's sex or sex and nationality, standing alone, is overbroad and insufficiently particular to be cognizable.
summary: This is higly relevant and impactful case law, in that PSG formulations such as 'Mexican women who XYZ' become immediately subject to a request for pre-termission by DHS.

name: Matter of A-L-S-
holding: (1) Flight risk encompasses not only whether a respondent is likely to appear at future hearings, but also whether the respondent is likely to comply with future orders of the Immigration Judge.
(2) Speculative future eligibility for relief does not materially diminish a finding of flight risk.
summary: Nuanced and specific: in A-L-S, the BIA reiterates the importance of flight risk for an IJ considering issuing a bond, and emphasizes that the mere fact that the respondent may have relief should not 'materially' reduce the risk of flight. While this may sound niche, many bond cases are borderline cases already.

name: Niz-Chavez v. Garland
holding: For purposes of triggering the stop-time rule for cancellation of removal, the government must serve a single Notice to Appear containing all statutorily required information. The required information cannot be supplied through multiple documents served at different times.
summary: Of tremendous significance to both practitioners, especially Respondents' counsel, as this Supreme Court decision further clarifies the way in which a person must be notified of the commencement of removal proceedings against them (through service of a Notice to Appear), as well as to Language Nerds, because this decision goes extremely hard regarding the murky grammar of the English language.

In any case, TL;DR: an NTA has to consist of one single, atomic, unitary document that includes both notice that the named person must appear for immigration proceedings, as well as the place, date, and time of that initial appearance. This sounds stupid and like 'yeah of course duh?' but, uh... It's harder to make a valid NTA than you would expect.

name: Matter of Buri Mora
summary: Addresses the 'exceptional and extremely unusual hardship' standard applicable to non-lawful permanent resident cancellation of removal under INA §240A(b).
notes: Clarifies application of the hardship standard. In particular, the existence of a qualifying relative's medical diagnosis, standing alone, does not automatically establish exceptional and extremely unusual hardship; the hardship determination remains a fact-intensive inquiry.

name: Matter of Josefina ARAMBULA-BRAVO, Respondent
holding: (1) A Notice to Appear that does not specify the time and place of a respondent's initial removal hearing does not deprive the Immigration Judge of jurisdiction over the respondent's removal proceedings.

(2) A Notice to Appear that lacks the time and place of a respondent's initial removal hearing constitutes a “charging document” as defined in 8 C.F.R. § 1003.13 (2021), and is sufficient to terminate a noncitizen's grant of parole under 8 C.F.R. § 212.5(e)(2)(i)(2021).
cites: Pereira v. Sessions, 138 S. Ct. 2105 (2018), and Niz-Chavez v. Garland, 141 S. Ct. 1474 (2021), distinguished; Matter of Bermudez-Cota, 27 I&N Dec. 441 (BIA 2018), and Matter of Rosales Vargas and Rosales Rosales, 27 I&N Dec. 745 (BIA 2020), followed.
summary: The next installment in the ongoing series, 'what is a notice to appear, anyway?', Arambula-Bravo specifies, among other things, that parole granted upon entry to the country is extinguished upon issuance of the NTA. This has additional consequences that may not be immediately apparent; it can, for example, change a certain legal status of a respondent, e.g. from 'arriving alien' to 'entered without inspection'. This can have effects on bond proceedings, sometimes preventing, or sometimes allowing for, bond to be set.

name: Matter of C-A-R-R-
holding: An Immigration Judge is not required to consider an Application for Asylum and for Withholding of Removal (Form I-589) on the merits if it is incomplete, and an incomplete application may be considered waived or abandoned, particularly where the respondent has been given an opportunity to cure the deficiency.

A declaration is not a constituent part of an asylum application. An Immigration Judge therefore may not deem a Form I-589 incomplete or abandoned solely because the respondent did not submit a declaration.
summary: C-A-R-R- addresses some conditions under which an Immigration Judge may treat an asylum application as incomplete and thereby consider it waived or abandoned. The I-589 itself--the actual freaking form, not a supplement pointed to with a note like 'see supplement'--must contain substantive answers to every question.

Importantly, however, a separate written declaration is not itself a required constituent part of Form I-589. Failure to submit a declaration therefore does not, standing alone, make the asylum application incomplete.
notes: This is, in a way, a long time coming, and represents a tremendously powerful tool for the DHS to request pre-termission of cases, thereby clearing out the cases that, `on their face`, are highly unlikely to prosper on their merits. The other tool, or horseman of the apocalypse depending on your politics, is Matter of H-A-A-V-, which addresses whether the facts alleged by the respondent in their application, even if accepted as true, establish prima facie eligibility for relief. One interesting thing to consider is the existence, in Spanish administrative law / case administration, of the legal figure 'aceptar a trámite'. This is a binary yes /no initial decisoin, generally made by a judge or similarly positioned legal expert, as to whether the case meets certain prima facie levels of sufficiency on given criteria. In a way -- if we can step back for a second -- the idea that the US Immigration courts went forward with a full hearing on applications that were wildly incomplete and whose alleged fact patterns clearly match existing case law barring the relief requested -- is a bit insane.

name: Matter of M-A-M-
holding: Respondents in immigration proceedings are presumed competent. If there are no indicia of incompetency, no further competency inquiry is required.

The test for competency is whether the respondent has a rational and factual understanding of the nature and object of the proceedings, can consult with an attorney or representative if there is one, and has a reasonable opportunity to examine and present evidence and cross-examine witnesses.
If there are indicia of incompetency, the Immigration Judge must make further inquiry to determine whether the respondent is competent for purposes of the proceedings.
If the respondent lacks sufficient competency to proceed, the Immigration Judge must evaluate appropriate safeguards.
Immigration Judges must articulate the rationale for their decisions regarding competency issues.
summary: This case created the case law which governs competency in immigration proceedings. M-A-M- establishes both the competency standard and the Immigration Judge's obligation to investigate competency when there are indicia that a respondent may not be competent.
notes: The way that this case law is put into practice is through what is literally called a 'MAM hearing'. This is confusing, of course, due to the existence of the Mayan language `Mam`, which is quite commonly seen in some US Immigration Courts, and the fact that the EOIR's internal 'language code' representing that language is, sigh, `MAM`, all caps. Of course, the citation for the case is `M-A-M-`, but when jurists refer to a `MAM hearing`, they leave the dashes out. Regardless of my issues with punctuation and proofreading: if the IJ finds that the respondent is not competent, the case doesn't just *go away*, the IJ implements safeguards to ensure that the respondent's rights are respected given the degree of their impairment.

name: INA § 237(a)(1)(B)
holding: A noncitizen who is present in the United States in violation of the Immigration and Nationality Act or any other law of the United States, or whose documentation authorizing admission as a nonimmigrant has been revoked, is deportable.
summary: One of the basic statutory grounds of deportability, in the old days, or what we now call removability. Section 237(a)(1)(B) applies to a person who is present in the United States in violation of immigration law or other federal law, including circumstances in which a person lawfully entered but no longer has authorization to remain.
notes: INA § 237 generally concerns grounds of deportability applicable after admission, in contrast with INA § 212, which contains grounds of inadmissibility.

name: INA § 212(a)(7)(A)(i)(I)
holding: Except as otherwise provided by law, an immigrant applying for admission who does not possess the required valid, unexpired immigrant visa, reentry permit, border crossing identification card, or other required entry document, together with any required valid passport or other suitable travel or identity document, is inadmissible.
summary: A documentation-based ground of inadmissibility applying to immigrants seeking admission to the United States without the documents required for lawful admission.

This provision belongs to INA § 212, the statutory collection of grounds of inadmissibility, rather than INA § 237's grounds of deportability. The INA-to-U.S.-Code correspondence  is: INA § 212 = 8 U.S.C. § 1182. Thus INA § 212(a)(7)(A)(i)(I) appears at 8 U.S.C. § 1182(a)(7)(A)(i)(I).
notes: The NTA review colloquy that IJs give regarding this charge is often formulated as follows: 'the Department (or Government) also alleges at the moment that you arrived/crossed the border/requested permission to enter/applied for admission to the United States, you were not then in possession of a valid, unexpired immigrant visa, re-entry permit, border crossing card, or other valid entry/immigration document as required by law. Is that true?'

name: Matter of M-A-F-
holding: Where an applicant filed an asylum application before the May 11, 2005 effective date of the REAL ID Act and subsequently files an application properly regarded as a new application, the filing date of the later application controls for determining whether the REAL ID Act's credibility provisions apply.
A subsequent asylum application is properly regarded as a new application when it presents a previously unraised basis for relief or is predicated on a new or substantially different factual basis.

Where multiple asylum applications have been filed and the later application constitutes a new application, the filing date of the later application controls for purposes of the one-year statutory filing deadline.
summary: M-A-F- addresses when a later-filed asylum application (an 'updated' I-589, when one has already been filed) should be considered to modify, complete, or otherwise update the existing claim, and when it instead constitutes a completely new factual basis and should be treated as a separate application.
notes: The distinction, well, 'it depends', of course, but if the updated 589 has new or different boxes checked for the protected ground on which the application's claim is based, and there are suddenly 300 pages of evidence (ie, you hadn't marked political opinion before, and you'd said vague things about crime in your country, and now it's political opinion and it turns out you were a candidate for political office targeted by government agents??), well--someone might start talking about matter of M-A-F-. Additionally, if the new 589 is considered to be a new application, this can change the date that is considered applicable for both REAL ID Act credibility rules and the asylum one-year filing deadline.

name: Matter of Graciela QUILANTAN, Respondent
holding: For purposes of establishing eligibility for adjustment of status under INA § 245(a), a noncitizen seeking to establish that he or she was 'admitted' under INA § 101(a)(13)(A) need only establish procedural regularity in the entry.
An admission does not require that immigration authorities question the person at the time of entry or that the person be admitted in a particular immigration status.
summary: Quilantan is the major case law behind the concept commonly described as being 'waved through' the border: a polemical concept that leaked out of the immigration law backrooms into public discourse, at least for a time. This results in certain circumstances in which persons are allowed to adjust status under INA § 245(a) even though they were not formally questioned, admitted, or otherwise assigned an immigration status -- in other words, they were 'waved through'. But only in certain circumstances.

The main factor is making a distinction between procedural regularity and substantive entitlement to enter. In other words, a person who physically presented themself for inspection and was permitted (waved, but not *waived*) through may have been 'admitted' for § 245(a) purposes even though they lacked documents that would ordinarily have entitled them to admission.

name: Matter of Monreal
holding: To establish 'exceptional and extremely unusual hardship' for non-LPR cancellation of removal under INA § 240A(b), an applicant must demonstrate that a qualifying spouse, parent, or child would suffer hardship substantially beyond that ordinarily expected to result from the applicant's removal, although the hardship need not be unconscionable.
The exceptional and extremely unusual hardship standard is more demanding than the former 'extreme hardship' standard applicable to suspension of deportation.

Only hardship to qualifying relatives may be considered in determining statutory eligibility for non-LPR cancellation; hardship to the applicant may be considered only insofar as it affects a qualifying relative.
summary: One of the foundational cases defining the 'exceptional and extremely unusual hardship' requirement for non-LPR cancellation of removal, aka 42-B relief. Monreal establishes that ordinary consequences of removal, even serious ones, are not enough; hardship to a qualifying relative must be substantially beyond what would ordinarily be expected.

The case also sharply limits whose hardship counts. The respondent's own hardship is not independently part of the statutory analysis, although circumstances affecting the respondent can matter insofar as they produce hardship for a qualifying U.S.-citizen or lawful-permanent-resident spouse, parent, or child.
notes: Frequently cited in 42B proceedings as a baseline statement of the hardship standard. It should be read alongside later hardship cases, particularly Matter of Andazola and Matter of Recinas.

name: Mendez Rojas v. Wolf
body: U.S. District Court, Western District of Washington
holding: As per the district court: the government's failure to provide adequate notice of the one-year asylum filing deadline and a meaningful filing mechanism violated legal requirements for affected class members.
summary: Class-action litigation concerning notice of the one-year asylum application deadline. A 2020 settlement established notice and filing procedures and time-limited relief for qualifying class members.

name: Matter of M-S-
holding: (1) Matter of X-K-, 23 I&N Dec. 731 (BIA 2005), was wrongly decided and is overruled.

(2) An alien who is transferred from expedited removal proceedings to full removal proceedings after establishing a credible fear of persecution or torture is ineligible for release on bond. Such an alien must be detained until his removal proceedings conclude, unless he is granted parole.
summary: If you were in expedited removal proceedings, and then your credible fear determination was positive, so they transferred you to full removal proceedings, the IJ does not have jurisdiction to grant you bond. You're going to stay detained until either your case is concluded, or DHS grants you parole--not bond.
notes: This might have been overturned--also, might not be applicable in all districts.

name: Matter of Acosta
holding: (1) Construction of the provisions the United Nations Protocol Relating to the Status of Refugees, Jan. 31, 1967, [1968 19 U.S.T. 6223, T.I.A.S. No. 6577, 606 U.N.T.S. 268, is left by that agreement to each state that is party to the Protocol; accordingly, the various international interpretations of the Protocol, including the Handbook on Procedures and Criteria for Determining Refugee Status Under the 1951 Convention and the 1967 Protocol Relating to the status of Refugees published by the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, are useful tools in construing our obligations under the Protocol, but they are neither binding upon the United States nor controlling as to construction of the Refugee Act of 1980.

(2) An alien in an exclusion or deportation proceeding who seeks to demonstrate eligibility for either asylum under section 208 of the Immigration and Nationality Act, 8 U.S.C. § 1158 (1982), or withholding of deportation under section 243(h) of the Act, 8 U.S.C. § 1253(h) (1982), must make two related showings: he must meet his evidentiary burdens of proof and persuasion as to the facts, and he must meet the statutory standards of eligibility set out by the pertinent provisions in the Act.
(3) It is the alien who bears the burdens of proof and persuasion in asylum and withholding of deportation cases and he must establish the facts by a preponderance of the evidence.

(4) In order to meet the statutory standard of eligibility for asylum, an alien must satisfy each of the following four elements in the definition of a refugee created by section 101(aX42XA) of the Act, 8 U.S.C. § 1101(aX42XA) (1982):
(1) the alien must have a 'fear' of 'persecution';
(2) the fear must be 'well founded';
(3) the persecution feared must be 'on account of race, religion, nationality, membership in a particular social group, or political opinion'; and
(4) the alien must be unable or unwilling to return to his country of nationality or to the country in which he last habitually resided because of persecution or his well-founded fear of persecution.

(5) The statutory standard for asylum requires the facts to show that an alien's primary motivation for requesting refuge in the United States is 'fear,' i e. , a genume apprehension or awareness of danger in another country, no other motivation will suffice.

(6) The term 'persecution' in the definition of a refugee under the Act means harm or suffering that is inflicted upon an individual in order to punish him for possessing a belief or characteristic a persecutor seeks to overcome; the word does not encompass the harm that arises out of civil or military strife in a country.

(7) The requirement of a 'well-founded fear of persecution' in section 101(aX42)(A) of the Act means that an individual's fear of persecution must have its basis in external, or objective, facts that show there is a realistic likelihood he will be persecuted upon his return to a particular country; this requires an alien to show that his fear has a solid basis in objective facts or events and that it is likely he will become the victim of persecution.
(8) In order for an alien to show that it is likely he will become the victim of persecution, his evidence must demonstrate that:
(1) the alien possesses a belief or characteristic a persecutor seeks to overcome in others by means of punishment of some sort;
(2) the persecutor is already aware, or could easily become aware, that the alien possesses this belief or characteristic;
(3) the persecutor has the capability of punishing the alien; and
(4) the persecutor has the inclination to punish the alien.
(9) The well-founded fear standard for asylum and the clear probability standard for withholding of deportation are not meaningfully different and, in practical application, converge.

(10) 'Persecution on account of membership in a particular social group' refers to persecution that is directed toward an individual who is a member of a group of persons, all of whom share a common, immutable characteristic. i.e., a characteristic that either is beyond the power of the individual members of the group to change or is so fundamental to their identities or consciences that it ought not be required to be changed.

(11) In order for an alien to show persecution on account of 'political opinion' within the meaning of the Act, it is not sufficient to show that a persecutor's conduct furthers his goals in a political controversy; rather, the alien must show that it is his own, individual political opinion that a persecutor seeks to overcome by the infliction of harm or suffering.

(12) The requirement that an alien must be unable or unwilling to return to a particular country because of persecution or a well-founded fear of persecution requires an alien to do more than show a threat of persecution in a particular place or abode within a country—he must show that the threat of persecution exists for him country-wide.
summary: Seminal, foundational case law, that anyone would be hard-pressed to summarize. This authority establishes the respondent's burden of proof; defines the standards of fear for asylum; specifies standards for persecution as it relates to Particular Social Groups; more tightly defines persecution on the basis of political opinion, and last but certainly not least, establishes that a threat of persecution must exist country-wide.
notes: While this authority's holdings echo through nearly every asylum case, there's been a lot of new law since. Regardless--foundational, required reading.

name: Matter of Zambrano
holding: (1) A more liberal policy toward divorce, as evidenced by the Divorce Reform Act of 1971, Stat. Ann. 2A:34-1, is now recognized in /slew Jersey. Kazin v. Kazin, Si N.J. 85, 405 A.2(1 360 (1979).
(2) New Jersey now appears to recognize foreign absentee divorces obtained by its residents. Matter of Guzman, 15 I&N Dec. 624 (BIA 1976), overruled in part.

(3) Where the record in visa petition proceedings was unclear whether the Dominican Republic divorce, alleged to constitute proof of the legal termination of the beneficiary's previous marriage and its pronouncement, was for cause or mutual consent, and it was unclear whether the formalities had been complied with, the record is remanded for further proceedings.
summary: Addresses recognition of foreign divorce decrees when determining the validity of a marriage supporting an immigrant visa petition.
notes: While it seems *oddly specific*, given the wide variety of contexts that exist under USCIS, all the different visas they issue (or don't), Zambrano continues to be relevant.

name: Rodriguez de Palucho v. Garland
body: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit
holding: In an asylum claim based on violence by private actors, the applicant must establish that the government is unable or unwilling to control the persecutors; the court rejected the claim on the record before it.
summary: A Sixth Circuit decision examining whether evidence of gang violence and government conduct established the required connection to state action through governmental inability or unwillingness to protect; affirms the BIA's underlying decisions.
notes: Circuit-specific. The case does not establish that a government must have advance knowledge of every threat before an asylum claim can succeed.

name: Velasquez v. Sessions
body: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit
holding: On the facts presented, a family custody dispute was a personal conflict rather than persecution on account of a protected ground; the applicant did not establish the required nexus.
summary: A highly specific fact pattern, but one that can be applied to a lot of situations. The case in question involved a truly acrimonious family conflict with terrible consequences. The Fourth Circuit affirmed that this situation in particular was an internal family dispute, and did not provide grounds for fear, persecution, or CAT-based protection.

name: Pereira v. Sessions
body: Supreme Court of the United States
holding: A notice to appear that fails to specify the time or place of a noncitizen's removal proceedings, as required by INA § 239(a)(1) (8 U.S.C. § 1229(a)(1)), does not trigger the stop-time rule under INA § 240A(d)(1) (8 U.S.C. § 1229b(d)(1)).

The statutory definition of a notice to appear requires, at a minimum for purposes of the stop-time rule, information identifying when and where the removal proceedings will be held. A document omitting that information does not satisfy the statutory requirement.

The statutory language governing notices to appear and the stop-time rule is unambiguous on this question. The government's administrative practice of issuing notices with hearing dates or locations to be determined does not override the requirements established by Congress.
summary: This is a chapter in the 'what is a valid NTA' saga: the prequel to Niz-Chavez. In a stunning bit of horrifically-difficult-to-translate legalese, this case concerns 'the stop-time rule'. That rule is about a part of 42-B cancellation of removal: the requirement that the applicant respondent to have been continuously physically present in the United States for a period of ten years prior to the service of the NTA. That service 'stops (the) time (count)' -- physical presence subsequent to the service of the NTA cannot be counted towards those ten years.

So, Pereira v. Sessions says that it's about the stop-time rule, but that's just a red herring. The case is actually about what makes a valid NTA, because a valid NTA is what triggers the stop-time rule. To Be Continued in the next chapter, Niz-Chavez v. Garland.
notes: At time of writing, the Supreme Court's .pdf posting of this authority 404s out: https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/17pdf/17-459_1o13.pdf. An alternate link is provided, but it of course may become defunct.

name: Matter of A-K-R-
holding: The Immigration Judge properly denied a further continuance to obtain counsel because the respondent had not shown good cause.
The statutory ten-day protection concerns the scheduling of the first hearing after service of the NTA; it does not create a general entitlement to repeated continuances. Matter of C-B- was modified.
summary: A 2026 BIA precedent concerning requests for additional time to secure legal representation and the minimum statutory preparation period following service of an NTA.
notes: The ten-day rule is not a ten-day cap on continuances. It refers to INA section 239(b)(1), concerning the first hearing after NTA service.

name: Matter of L-A-B-R-
holding: In evaluating good cause for a continuance to pursue collateral relief, an Immigration Judge should focus principally on the likelihood that the collateral relief will be granted and whether it would materially affect the outcome of removal proceedings.
The judge must also consider relevant secondary factors, including diligence, DHS's position, administrative efficiency, prior continuances, and the timing and length of the requested continuance.
summary: An Attorney General decision setting out a structured good-cause analysis for continuances requested while a respondent pursues relief in another adjudicative process.
notes: The rule concerns collateral-relief continuances, not every possible reason to seek additional preparation time.

name: Matter of Lozada
holding: An ineffective-assistance claim supporting a motion to reopen or reconsider ordinarily requires a detailed affidavit describing the representation agreement and alleged deficiencies.
Prior counsel must be informed of the allegations and given an opportunity to respond.
The motion must state whether a disciplinary complaint was filed against prior counsel and, if not, explain why.
summary: Establishes the procedural framework commonly used to evaluate ineffective-assistance-of-counsel allegations in immigration proceedings. A Lozada motion typically seeks to remedy prejudice from deficient prior representation.
notes: A 'Lozada motion' is not a separate statutory form of motion. It commonly refers to a motion to reopen alleging ineffective assistance, with the procedural showing required by this precedent.
